code.title: Lazy chunk loading with cache and retry

followUps:
You write a class that implements PreloadingStrategy and decides per route whether to call the loader.

Mark routes with data, then preload only those:

preload(route, load) {
  return route.data?.preload ? load() : of(null);
}

Register it with withPreloading(MyStrategy). You can also add a delay (timer(2000).pipe(mergeMap(load))) or skip preloading on slow connections via navigator.connection.saveData. This keeps the first load small but makes likely next pages instant.

The browser asks for an old file name that no longer exists, so the dynamic import fails and the navigation errors out.

Fixes: catch the error in the router error handler or a global ErrorHandler and do one full location.reload() to pick up the new build (guard it with a flag so you never loop). Keep old chunks on the server for a while after a deploy, and use hashed file names with long cache lifetimes for chunks only. The demo shows the retry-once idea: a failure is never cached.

Use loadComponent for one page and loadChildren for a whole feature with its own child routes.

With loadComponent: () => import('./about').then(m => m.About) you get one chunk with no extra route file. With loadChildren: () => import('./admin/routes').then(m => m.ADMIN_ROUTES) the feature owns its route array, its guards and its providers, so the parent stays small. Pick loadChildren when a section has several routes or section-wide providers.

code.title: canMatch vs canActivate redirect

followUps:
Because they depend on inheritance and injection of a class, while functions are simpler, tree-shakable and easy to compose.

A class guard needs @Injectable, a constructor and a provider; a functional guard is just const auth: CanActivateFn = () => inject(AuthService).ok() || inject(Router).parseUrl('/login'). Functions can be reused across routes with small factories like hasRole('admin'). Angular deprecated the class interfaces (CanActivate and friends) in v15.2 and removed them in a later major.

Call it inside TestBed.runInInjectionContext so that inject() works, and provide fake services.

TestBed.configureTestingModule({providers:[{provide:AuthService,useValue:{ok:()=>false}}]});
const r = TestBed.runInInjectionContext(() => authGuard(route, state));
expect(r.toString()).toBe('/login');

Assert on the returned value: true, or a UrlTree whose string you compare. For observable results, subscribe or use firstValueFrom.

Parent guards run before child guards, and the router checks them top-down; the first failure stops the navigation.

The order is: canMatch while matching, then canDeactivate on routes being left (deepest first), then canActivateChild and canActivate parent to child on routes being entered. Then resolvers run, and only then the components activate. By default guards of one level run in parallel, but a redirect (UrlTree) from any of them cancels the current navigation and starts a new one.

Listen to router events and show a bar between the start and the end of navigation.

Resolvers keep the old page visible, so users need feedback. Subscribe to router.events, set a navigating signal to true on NavigationStart and false on NavigationEnd, NavigationCancel and NavigationError. Missing the last two is the common bug: the bar then spins forever after a failed resolver. Put the bar in the app shell so every route gets it.

Turn on withComponentInputBinding() in provideRouter and declare an input named like the resolver key.

For resolve: { user: userResolver } the component writes user = input.required<User>(). The same mechanism also binds path params, query params and data. If names clash, the order is data first, then resolve, then params. This replaces ActivatedRoute.data subscriptions with plain inputs, which works well with OnPush and signals.

Because they get their control tree from directives that run after the first render, so the controls are created a moment later.

With ngModel, Angular creates each FormControl in a resolved Promise (a microtask) to avoid changing the form during change detection. So right after the view is created, form.controls.name can still be undefined. Reactive forms build the controls in your class constructor, so value and validity are available synchronously. That is why reactive forms are simpler to test.

With typed forms, reset() sets a control to its initial value only if you use a non-nullable control; otherwise it sets null.

A plain new FormControl('a') has type string | null and reset() gives null. new FormControl('a', {nonNullable: true}) (or NonNullableFormBuilder) resets back to 'a' and keeps the type string. You can also pass a value: ctrl.reset('b').

getRawValue() returns the values of all controls, including disabled ones, which value leaves out.

Example: a group with id (disabled, 7) and name ('Ann'). form.value is {name:'Ann'}, but form.getRawValue() is {id:7, name:'Ann'}. Use it when you display read-only fields you still need to send, and prefer it with typed forms because its type has no optional keys.

It is needed when you refer to a class inside its own decorator, before the class is defined.

In providers: [{provide: NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR, useExisting: StarsComponent}], the identifier StarsComponent is evaluated when the decorator runs, which is before the class binding is initialised, so you would get a ReferenceError or undefined. forwardRef(() => StarsComponent) delays the lookup until it is needed. In modern setups with a standalone component it is still the safe default.

Inject the control with NgControl and read its state, instead of providing NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR yourself.

Set ngControl.valueAccessor = this in the constructor (with @Self()), then in the template use ngControl.invalid && ngControl.touched to show a message from ngControl.errors. Remember that this injection replaces the provider approach, and that OnPush needs markForCheck() when status changes, for example via statusChanges.

code.title: Debounced async validator

followUps:
Because Angular cancels the previous validator subscription each time the value changes, and timer only emits after the delay.

If the user types 5 letters within 400 ms, each keystroke starts a new timer(400) and unsubscribes the old one, so only the last timer fires and switchMap makes one HTTP call. The demo shows 5 keystrokes producing 1 server call. This only works inside the validator, where Angular does the unsubscribing.

Take the field error from the server response and call control.setErrors({usernameTaken: true}).

error: e => {
  if (e.status === 409)
    form.controls.username.setErrors({ usernameTaken: true });
}

The error stays until the next validation run, which clears it when the user edits the value. Mark the control touched so the message shows, and still keep client-side checks for fast feedback.

code.title: OnPush needs a new reference

followUps:
It means a binding changed value after Angular had already checked it, usually because a child or a lifecycle hook changed parent state during the same pass.

In dev mode Angular runs a second check and compares; if a value differs (for example a child sets a parent field in ngAfterViewInit), it throws. Fixes: compute the value earlier, use a signal or computed, or move the change into the next tick (afterNextRender). It exists only in dev mode, but the bug it points to is real.

Signals tell Angular exactly which view read a changed signal, so that view is refreshed without checking the whole tree.

A template that reads count() registers a dependency. When count.set(2) runs, only that component is marked for refresh (and its ancestors up to the root are walked, not re-evaluated). Other OnPush components are skipped. Without signals, a click anywhere marks the path dirty and checks everything on it.

markForCheck() schedules a check for the next normal pass; detectChanges() runs a check on this view right now.

Use markForCheck after async work in an OnPush component (a subscription callback): it marks the path to the root dirty and Angular does the rest. detectChanges is synchronous and only for this view and its children, so overusing it causes extra work and can throw in destroyed views. Default choice: markForCheck, or just use a signal.

Anything that changes state without telling Angular: the screen simply does not update.

Examples: a plain field changed inside setTimeout, a third-party library callback, or subscribe that sets a normal property. With zones, the timer end triggered a check automatically; zoneless does not. Nothing throws, the UI is just stale. Fix by using signals, the async pipe, or markForCheck(). Tests that relied on fixture.detectChanges() side effects also need whenStable.

Since v18 even zone-based apps also schedule change detection from signal writes and markForCheck, not only from zone events.

The scheduler batches those notifications and runs one check in the next tick, whichever source (zone or Angular's own notification) fires first. It means components written with signals already work and update correctly in a zone app, which makes later removal of zone.js a smaller step. Enable by default in v18+; you can opt out with ignoreChangesOutsideZone settings.

On the server, @defer renders the @placeholder block, not the deferred content.

Triggers like viewport or interaction need a browser, so the server cannot know when they fire. The HTML then contains the placeholder (same size, ideally). With incremental hydration and hydrate on ..., the server can instead render the real content and the client only attaches JavaScript later. So choose between a placeholder-only deferred block, or a server-rendered block hydrated on demand.

A lazy route splits by URL and loads when you navigate; @defer splits inside a page and loads when its trigger fires.

Use a route for whole screens (admin, reports). Use @defer for a part of the current screen, such as a chart below the fold, that may never be seen. @defer also gives you built-in placeholder, loading and error blocks and triggers (viewport, idle, hover, timer) without writing loader code.

Compare the server HTML with what the client template would render, and look at the error message first.

Angular's NG0500 family names the component and the expected and actual node. Typical causes: invalid HTML nesting (a <div> inside a <p>), direct DOM changes, or values like Date.now() and Math.random() that differ per environment. Fix by moving browser-only code into afterNextRender, using stable values, or adding ngSkipHydration to a stubborn component as a last resort.

Choose prerendering when the page is the same for everyone and can be built at deploy time, such as marketing pages and docs.

A prerendered page is a static file served from a CDN: fastest TTFB, no server cost, no server to scale. SSR is needed when HTML depends on the request (user, cookies, live data). With per-route render modes you can mix: RenderMode.Prerender for /about, RenderMode.Server for /account. Prerender is not suitable for content that changes every minute.

It stores the HTTP responses made on the server and reuses them in the browser so the client does not request the same data again.

Without it, SSR fetches /api/products on the server, the page hydrates, and the browser fetches the same URL again, which is a wasted request and may flash different data. provideClientHydration() turns it on for HttpClient GET and HEAD calls. It is keyed by URL and params, and you can filter what is cached.

Start with local component state, then URL state, then a shared service, and add a store only when a feature really needs it.

Ask for each piece of state: who else reads it? If only one component, keep it in a signal there. If it is a filter or page, keep it in the URL so links work. Server data belongs in a cache layer (httpResource or a query library). A global store should hold only shared client state, such as the current user or a cart.

Migrate one feature at a time, keeping the old store running next to the new SignalStores.

Steps: pick a leaf feature, create a signalStore with the same state shape, expose the same selectors as computed signals, and replace store.select with the new store in its components. Bridge in between using toSignal(store.select(...)) or store.dispatch from the new methods. Delete the feature's actions, reducer and effects only after nothing reads them.

code.title: Latest search wins (switchMap idea)

followUps:
Put catchError inside the inner observable of switchMap, not on the outer stream.

switchMap(q => api.search(q).pipe(
  map(r => loadSuccess({ r })),
  catchError(e => of(loadFailure({ e })))
))

An error that reaches the outer stream completes it, and the effect stops listening, so later searches do nothing. Inside, only that one request ends, and the effect lives on.

Use concatMap when every action must run, in order, and none may be dropped, like saving edits.

Example: the user clicks "save" three times with different data. switchMap would cancel the first two requests; concatMap runs 1, then 2, then 3. exhaustMap ignores new clicks while one is running (login button), and mergeMap runs all in parallel without order guarantees.

Test it with a fake actions stream, a mock API and the marble tester or simple subscribe.

actions$ = of(searchChanged({ q: 'a' }));
api.search.mockReturnValue(of([1]));
effect(actions$, api).subscribe(a =>
  expect(a).toEqual(loadSuccess({ r: [1] })));

Add a second test where the mock throws and expect loadFailure, and check the effect still handles a following action. Use TestScheduler to test debounce and cancellation with virtual time.

Because a method in a template runs on every change detection pass, even when its inputs did not change.

If a row uses {{ format(row) }} and the grid has 500 rows, one keystroke triggers 500 calls, and each may allocate arrays or strings. A pure pipe or a computed signal caches the result and reruns only when its input changes. Moving the formatting to such a cache cuts 500 calls per keystroke to 1 for the changed row.

Virtual scrolling renders only visible rows, so it needs a known row height and takes extra care for screen readers.

The CDK viewport uses a fixed itemSize (for example 40 px) to compute the scroll height; variable heights need the autosize strategy, which is less accurate. Browser search (Ctrl+F) and screen readers cannot see rows that are not in the DOM, so set aria-rowcount and aria-rowindex, and offer a search box and pagination as an alternative.

code.title: Filter, sort, paginate users

followUps:
Make the router own them: write query params when the user changes sort or page, and read them back as the source of truth.

Use router.navigate([], {queryParams: {q, sort, page}, queryParamsHandling: 'merge'}) and read with withComponentInputBinding() or toSignal(route.queryParamMap). Debounce the search text before writing it. Benefits: refresh and back button work, and links can be shared. Use replaceUrl: true for typing so history does not fill up.

I would test the pure logic first: filtering, sorting and paging.

It is cheap and catches the most bugs: for example "ad" matches Adrian and Ada case-insensitively, sort does not change the original array, and the page is clamped when the filter shrinks the list (page 5 of 2 becomes 2). Then one component test for loading, empty and error states, then a test that changing the query resets the page to 1.

With 1 million rows, stop loading everything in the browser: filter, sort and page on the server and send only one page.

The component then sends q, sort, page and size to the API (debounced, with switchMap to drop stale replies) and gets back {rows, total}. Add an index on the sorted column, and use cursor paging if offsets become slow. If the grid must scroll continuously, add virtual scrolling with chunked loading.
